text:
BRUSSELS — U.S. deputy Pentagon chief Elbridge Colby on Tuesday hit out at Ukraine for its long-range strike campaign against Russia — a fresh blow to Kyiv as it seeks to shore up its negotiating position during peace talks with Moscow.
His comments, made at a meeting primarily aimed at raising further support for Ukraine, come as the U.S. is expected to hold fresh peace negotiations with Ukraine and Russia in the coming weeks.
“While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective … nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line,” Colby said at a meeting of the Ukrainian Defense Contact Group defense ministers in Brussels.
“Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure ... have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate,” he said, adding: “The balance of advantage in deep strikes may well favor Moscow.”
The comments prompted an immediate rebuke from Ukraine’s NATO allies.
“Criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military … targets is quite a stupid thing,” German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius said after the meeting. “Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about [Russia’s] terroristic strikes every night.”
“It's not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters. “In terms of deep strike capability, there's no doubt in my mind that it's helped to degrade [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's war machine.”
Ukraine has in recent months stepped up long-range attacks deep inside Russia, targeting depots of the online retailer Wildberries, military facilities, oil refineries and fuel export facilities. It says it has taken out 30% of Russian oil refining capacity. On Tuesday, Ukraine said it had destroyed part of the Kerch bridge linking Russia to Crimea.
Washington has long opposed deep strikes against Russia, particularly those that affect oil infrastructure. U.S. President Donald Trump last month accused Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. Zelenskyy has previously said the strikes give Ukraine “equal footing” in negotiations with Russia.
Colby urged ministers to keep funding the NATO-backed PURL program, where Ukrainian allies pay for American weapons for Kyiv. “Sustaining the flow of critical munitions is essential for Ukrainian troops to continue holding the front line,” he said.
PURL was set up last year after the U.S. stopped directly funding Ukraine's war effort following Trump's return to power.
On Tuesday, several countries including Germany, Norway and Sweden announced over $300 million in fresh contributions to the scheme. The U.K. separately announced £240 million in air defense support, including over 1,000 short-range missiles and a dozen air defense radars.
NATO allies are still billions short of meeting a €70 billion alliance military aid target for Ukraine this year, and a separate goal of raising at least €12 billion for PURL. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte told POLITICO he was “cautiously optimistic” allies could still meet the overall target, set at the alliance’s July summit in Ankara.
Despite the criticism of long-range strikes, Colby praised Ukraine’s “very effective” use of mid-range strike drones to “deny Russian advances” on the front line.
Ukraine last week said it had detected limitations on critical U.S. Starlink satellite services for the second time in two months, a move Kyiv said made it more difficult to intercept Russian drones.
Asked about the latest restrictions, Colby demurred, telling reporters: “We are very focused on supporting Ukraine's ability to defend itself and these … mid-range strikes, and we're taking steps that are consistent with that policy.”
